topic: Return Value Optimization (RVO) and Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO)
explanation: Return Value Optimization (RVO) and its more specific form, Named Return Value Optimization (NRVO), are compiler optimizations that eliminate unnecessary object copies when returning objects by value from functions.  Instead of creating a temporary object on the stack and then copying it to the caller's location, the compiler directly constructs the object in the caller's memory location. This significantly impacts performance, especially for large or complex objects.  The compiler's ability to perform RVO/NRVO depends heavily on the function's structure and the object's nature.  Specifically, the compiler analyzes the return statement and the caller's context to determine if it's safe to perform this optimization.  If the returned object is a temporary or unnamed, RVO is possible; if the object has a name in the return statement, NRVO is possible.  Failure to perform RVO/NRVO results in an extra object creation and copy, leading to increased memory usage and execution time.  The optimization is heavily reliant on compiler heuristics; different compilers might produce different assembly code and may or may not perform the optimization depending on their settings and complexity of the return value.
code_example: MyClass(const std::string& str) : str_(str) { std::cout << "MyClass constructed\n"; }
MyClass(const MyClass& other) : str_(other.str_) { std::cout << "MyClass copy-constructed\n"; }
example_explanation: In the example, if RVO/NRVO is performed, the output will only show one "MyClass constructed" and one "MyClass destructed".  If the compiler doesn't perform the optimization, we would see "MyClass constructed", "MyClass copy-constructed", and two "MyClass destructed" statements.  Analyzing the generated assembly code can confirm if RVO/NRVO occurred. The presence (or absence) of instructions related to memory allocation and copying for `MyClass` objects will indicate whether the optimization was applied. Different compiler optimization levels will impact whether RVO/NRVO is utilized and will significantly change assembly code.  Disabling optimizations entirely prevents RVO/NRVO. Using a debugger to examine the creation and destruction of MyClass objects is another way to observe whether or not RVO/NRVO occurred.
